```{r}
#| eval: false

fname<-here::here("Data", "chep.zip")
if(!file.exists(fname)){
  download.file('https://civichealth.norc.org/downloads/civichealth_datafile.zip',
                mode='wb',
                dest=fname
  )
}

chep<-read_dta(unz(fname, filename='civichealth_datafile.dta' ))

# Converting to factors
chep_fac<-chep|>
  as_factor()

labs<-labelled::var_label(chep)

labsframe<-tibble(variable = names(labs), description = unname(labs))

# Converting to factors
chep_fac<-chep|>
  as_factor()


# Calculating hardship index
chep_fac$HARDSHIP_INDEX<-chep_fac|>
  select(starts_with("FINANCE"))|>
  select(-FINANCE_NONE)|>
  mutate(across(everything(), .fns=~as.numeric(.x)-1))|>
  rowSums()


# subsetting, recoding, and dropping some missing data
chep_subset<-chep_fac|>
  #filter(VOTE24_CHOICE %in% c("(1) Kamala Harris","(2) Donald Trump"))|>
  filter(VOTE24_CHOICE != "(99) DON'T KNOW/SKIPPED/REFUSED")|>

  select(VOTE24_CHOICE, HOUSEVOTE, AGE6, EDUC, INCOME, RACETH4, HARDSHIP_INDEX, CHEP_WEIGHT, AIFAV_LOCALDATA,
         PARTYFULL, SEX, starts_with("FINANCE"))|>
  mutate(across(c("AGE6", "EDUC", "INCOME", "RACETH4", "AIFAV_LOCALDATA", "SEX"), .fns=~replace_values(.x, 
                                                                            c("(99) DON'T KNOW/SKIPPED/REFUSED") ~ NA)
                
                ),
         across(c("AGE6","RACETH4"), .fns=~replace_values(.x, 
                                                                            c("(88) REMOVED FOR DISCLOSURE RISK") ~ NA))
         
         )|>
  droplevels()|>
  mutate(REPVOTE = case_when(HOUSEVOTE == "(2) Republican candidate for Congress" ~ "Yes",
                             HOUSEVOTE != "(2) Republican candidate for Congress" ~ "No" 
                             
                             )|>factor(),
         AIFAV_LOCALDATA_NUMERIC = as.numeric(AIFAV_LOCALDATA)
         
         )|>
  # dropping missing data (we lose a lot here which is probably not great! but
  # we're going to ignore that for the sake of simplicity)
  drop_na()

labs<-labs[colnames(chep_subset)[which(colnames(chep_subset)%in%names(labs))]]

labelled::var_label(chep_subset) <- labs

labelled::var_label(chep_subset$HARDSHIP_INDEX) <- "Financial Hardship Index"
labelled::var_label(chep_subset$REPVOTE) <- "Did R vote for Republican Candidate in the House?"
labelled::var_label(chep_subset$VOTE24_CHOICE) <- "2024 Presidential Vote"


saveRDS(chep_subset, file=here::here("Data", "chep_subset.rds"))
```

## Linear models

How should we model outcomes that are non-continuous?

- The "Time spent on childcare" measured on the American Time Use survey is always a non-negative integer value.

- Responses to a "yes/no" question can be treated as 0 and 1, but they're still discrete outcomes.

- Responses on a Likert scale might be ordered from 1 to 5, but they're technically not continuous.

::: fragment
Linear models will typically be a poor fit for this kind of outcome.

:::


## Generalized Linear Models


Generalized Linear Models (GLM) are a way of extending the Linear Modeling framework to fit models with all sorts of distributions.

::: fragment
Every GLM has three components:

1. A specific [probability distribution]{.yellow} (Y) for the outcome variable. Such as: normal, binomial, poisson, gamma etc.

2. A systematic component ($\eta$) that is a linear function of the independent variables (this looks like a linear model $\eta = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_1 + \beta_2X_2...$)

3. A link function $g$ that transforms the linear component into the expected value on the outcome scale (and that can be inverted to transform the outcome back to the linear scale.)

:::

## Notation note

We'll use some matrix notation here just to make things a bit more readable. Just note that this:

$$
X'\beta
$$

Is the same thing as the linear model we've been writing:

$$
\beta_0 + \beta_1X_1 + \beta_2X_2... = 
$$



## Linear models and Binary Outcomes



To make the problem more concrete, we can use some recently released polling data from the NORC Civic Health & Elections Project to look at modeling vote choice.


::: fragment
As usual, we're going to initially ignore the survey weights initially, but we'll bring those back into the analysis in a bit.

:::


## NORC Data


::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

::: non-incremental


::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

Respondents were asked a series of questions about financial hardships experienced within the last year.
:::

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="2"}


These were combined to create an additive index of "financial hardship"

:::

:::

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

:::: {.r-stack}


::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="1" .fade-in-then-out}

```{r}
library(gt)
library(srvyr)
library(survey)

chep_yesno <- chep_subset|>
  mutate(CHEP_WEIGHT = CHEP_WEIGHT * (n()/sum(CHEP_WEIGHT)) )|>
  select(starts_with("FINANCE_"), CHEP_WEIGHT)|>
    select(-FINANCE_NONE)|>
  pivot_longer(cols=-CHEP_WEIGHT)|>
  group_by(name, value)|>
  summarise(CHEP_WEIGHT = sum(CHEP_WEIGHT))|>
  group_by(name)|>
  mutate(wtd_prop = (CHEP_WEIGHT/sum(CHEP_WEIGHT)))|>
  ungroup()|>
  select(-CHEP_WEIGHT)|>
  pivot_wider(names_from =  value, values_from =wtd_prop)

chep_yesno$label<- labelled::var_label(chep_subset[chep_yesno$name])|>unname()|>unlist()
chep_yesno|>
  mutate(label = str_replace(label, "In the past year, have you done or experienced any of the following\\? ", ""))|>
  select(Question = label, No = `(0) Not selected`, Yes=`(1) Selected`)|>
  arrange(Yes)|>
  select(Question, Yes)|>
  gt()|>
  fmt_percent(decimals=0)|>
  cols_label(Question = md("**In the past year, have you done or experienced any of the following?**"))|>
  tab_source_note("Source: NORC Civic Health & Elections Project 2026")
  
```

:::

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="2"}

```{r}

chep_subset|>
  mutate(CHEP_WEIGHT = CHEP_WEIGHT * (n()/sum(CHEP_WEIGHT)) )|>
  select(HARDSHIP_INDEX, CHEP_WEIGHT)|>
  group_by(HARDSHIP_INDEX)|>
  summarise(num = sum(CHEP_WEIGHT))|>
  ungroup()|>
  mutate(prop = num/sum(num))|>
  ggplot(aes(x=HARDSHIP_INDEX, y=prop)) + geom_col() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(y='Weighted Percent',
       x = "Number of financial hardships",
       subtitle = "Number of financial hardships in the last year",
       caption = "Source: NORC Civic Health & Elections Project 2026"
       )

  
```

## Modeling a dichotomous outcome

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
I want to look at the effects of the hardship index on the probability of voting for the Republican candidate in their local congressional race.
:::

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="2"}
I suspect past vote choice may be a confounding variable here, so I also want to control for 2024 vote.
:::

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}


:::: {.r-stack}
::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="1" .fade-in-then-out}

```{r}

chep_subset|>
  group_by(HARDSHIP_INDEX)|>
  summarise(prop = sum(REPVOTE=="Yes")/n(),
            wtd_prop = sum(CHEP_WEIGHT[which(REPVOTE=="Yes")])/sum(CHEP_WEIGHT)
            )|>
ggplot(aes(x=HARDSHIP_INDEX, y=wtd_prop)) + 
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +

       x ="Number of Financial Hardships Experienced",
       title = "House vote in 2026",
       subtitle = "by number of financial difficulties in last year",
       caption = "Source: NORC Civic Health & Elections Project 2026",
       ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent())

```

```{r}
chep_subset|>

ggplot(aes(x=HARDSHIP_INDEX, y=wtd_prop, color=VOTE24_CHOICE)) +
```

## Modeling a dichotomous outcome

If I convert the yes/no outcome to 1s and 0s, I can still fit a linear model even though the outcome isn’t continuous:

```{r}
#| echo: true
chep_subset$repvote_numeric<-as.numeric(chep_subset$REPVOTE=="Yes")
model<-lm(repvote_numeric ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE,data= chep_subset)

```

## Modeling a dichotomous outcome


::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
The coefficients here can be interpreted as the effect of a one unit increase on each variable on the probability of voting for the Republican in 2026.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}

```{r}
lm(repvote_numeric ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE,data= chep_subset)|>
  summary()


```

```{r}
library(modelsummary)
chep_subset$repvote_numeric<-as.numeric(chep_subset$REPVOTE=="Yes")
model<-lm(repvote_numeric ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE,data= chep_subset)


modelsummary(list("2026 House Vote" = model), 
             coef_rename = TRUE,
             fmt = 3,  
             statistic = "conf.int",

)
```

## Modeling a dichotomous outcome



::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
This is the key problem with fitting a linear model to an outcome that isn't continuous: the outcome here just can't really be modeled with a line.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
preds|>
  filter(group  == "(1) Kamala Harris")|>
  plot(colors='blue') + 
  ylab("predicted %") + 
  labs(title = "Predicted % Voting for Republican",

       ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 13, by = 1)) +
    scale_color_manual(values=c("blue","#DC143C", "purple", "grey"))+
  heiss_theme 

```
:::
:::::





## Generalized Linear Models: dichotomous outcomes

We still want to retain the linear modeling framework $y= X'\beta$, but we need a function that can transform a straight line into something with these properties:

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- The function should take any real number as an input and map it onto a 0, 1 range.

- Ideally, we'd like to capture the "diminishing returns" of changes when the probability of y is really high or really low. 



:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}

preds|>
  filter(group  == "(1) Kamala Harris")|>
  plot(colors='blue') + 
  ylab("predicted %") + 
  labs(title = "Predicted % Voting for Republican",
       subtitle = "Harris Voters only"
       ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 13, by = 1)) +
    scale_color_manual(values=c("blue","#DC143C", "purple", "grey"))+
  heiss_theme 
```


```{r}

set.seed(123)


# 1. Define sample size and parameters
n <- 100
beta_0 <- -1.0   # Intercept
beta_1 <- -0.7    # Slope for predictor x
# 2. Generate a random predictor variable (e.g., normal or uniform)
x <- runif(n, min=-10, max=10)
# 3. Calculate log-odds (logit of probabilities)
log_odds <- beta_0 + beta_1 * x
# 4. Convert log-odds to probabilities using the inverse-logit (sigmoid) function
p <- 1 / (1 + exp(-log_odds))
# 5. Generate binary response variable (0 or 1) using a binomial distribution
y <- rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = p)

            newdata =data.frame(x=min(x), max(x), by=.1)
# Combine into a data frame
sim_data <- data.frame(x = x, log_odds = log_odds, prob = p, y = y)

#ggplot(data=sim_data,aes(x=x, y=y))+ 
#  geom_point() +
 # geom_smooth(method='lm', se=FALSE)


```
:::
:::::


## Generalized Linear Models: dichotomous outcomes


::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- The logistic function $p = \frac{1}{1+e^{-(X'\beta)}}$ maps a linear prediction back to the probability scale.

- This amounts to modeling $\log{\frac{p}{1-p}} = \beta ' X$ or the logged odds of y=1. 

- This gives us the [logit model]{.yellow}.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
invlogit<-function(x){
  ret<-1/(1+exp(-x))
  return(ret)
}

ggplot() +
  xlim(-10, 10) +
  geom_function(fun = invlogit, color = "blue", linewidth = 1) +
  xlab("logged odds") +
  ylab("probability")

```
:::
:::::




## Generalized Linear Models: dichotomous outcomes


::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Another option is to use $\Phi(XB)$ where  $\Phi$ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function (the same integral math that turns a z-score into a probability under the normal distribution)

- This gives us the [probit model]{.yellow}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
invprobit<-function(x){
  x<-pnorm(x)
}

ggplot() +
  xlim(-10, 10) +
  geom_function(fun = invprobit, color = "red", linewidth = 1,lty=2) +
  xlab("probit") +
  ylab("probability")

```
:::
:::::



## Logit and probit



::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Both the [logit]{.yellow} and [probit]{.yellow} models will give us a result that is bounded between 0 and 1.

- The logit model has slightly "fatter tails", but, in practice, the results tend to be substantively very similar.

- Today, logit models are more common because they have a slightly more intuitive interpretation than probit models.


:::
::: {.column width="50%"}




```{r}
ggplot() +
  xlim(-10, 10) +
  geom_function(fun = invprobit, color = "blue", linewidth = 1,) +
  geom_function(fun = invlogit, color = "red", linewidth = 1, lty=2) +
  xlab("") +
  ylab("probability")
```


:::
:::::


## Generalized Linear Models: dichotomous outcomes

So, now we've got everything we need for a generalized linear model:

1. Our outcome has a binomial distribution where everything is a 1 or a 0.

2. We have a systematic component that can be defined with a linear model $\eta= X'B$

3. We have a function (such as logit) that can map $\eta$ onto the response scale.

## Fitting GLMs

In a linear model, we can identify the line of best fit by minimizing the sum of squared residuals, but there's no real analog for this with a GLM.

So how do I know whether one model is better than any other?


## Fitting GLMs: Maximum Likelihood

- Rather than minimizing the sum of squared errors, most generalized linear models will find the best fit using [Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)]{.yellow}

- In MLE, we find the set of parameter values (typically denoted using the symbol $\theta$) that are *most likely* to have generated the data we see.




## Fitting GLMs: Maximum Likelihood


We'll look at a simple application to get a sense of how MLE works: finding the maximum likelihood estimate of a population proportion from a sample proportion.



## MLE of a proportion


- Imagine a survey of 100 randomly selected adults finds that about 26% believe in Bigfoot 

- What is the population probability of Bigfoot belief ($\theta$) that is [most likely]{.yellow} to have generated this result?


## MLE of a proportion

$\theta$ *could* be any number $>0$  and $<1$. It's *possible* to get a sample where 26% believe in Bigfoot even if the population percent is 40%:


```{r}
#| cache: true
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 6
set.seed(1000)

df<-data.frame(x=rbinom(1e6, 100, .40))

ggplot(df, aes(x=x)) + geom_histogram() +
  geom_vline(xintercept=26, lty=2, color='red') +
  labs(title = "1 million simulated samples",
       subtitle = "n = 100; θ = .40",
     xlab="Number of sampled respondents who believe in Bigfoot")

```




::: fragment

You can probably already guess that the correct answer here is $\theta = .26$, but we want a way to *systematically* pick the best value of $\theta$ for more complicated problems.

:::

## MLE of a proportion


Since "belief in Bigfoot" is a simple yes/no question, then we can model a single response using the Bernoulli Probability Mass Function:

$$
\begin{align*}
P(y_i=1|\theta) = \theta^{y_i}(1-\theta)^{1-y_i}\\
\theta = \text{probability that y is 1}\\
y_i = \text{a single response to the question}
\end{align*}
$$


. . .


So, if $y_i=1$ and $\theta = .20$

$$
P(1|.20) = .20^{1}(.75)^{0} = .20
$$


. . .


If $y_i=0$ and $\theta = .20$ 

$$
P(0|.20) = .20^{0}(.80)^{1} = .80
$$

## MLE of a proportion

Assuming that the observations are all independent and identically distributed, we can calculate the *likelihood* of the entire sample by simply multiplying together all the individual probabilities from each of the 100 observations:

$$
L(y|\theta) =  \prod^n_{i=1} \theta^{y_i}(1-\theta)^{1-y_i} = \theta^{\sum{y_i}}(1-\theta)^{n-\sum{y_i}}
$$


## MLE of a proportion

$$
L(y|\theta) =  \prod^n_{i=1} \theta^{y_i}(1-\theta)^{1-y_i} = \theta^{\sum{y_i}}(1-\theta)^{n-\sum{y_i}}
$$

We run into a bit of a computational problem here because we're multiplying a bunch of probabilities, this gets very small very quickly.

```{r}
#| echo: true

.25 * .25 * .75 * .25 * .25 * .25 * .75 * .25 # ... and so on

```


::: fragment

Using a logarithm gets around this problem by turning the tiny fractions into large negative numbers, and allowing us to use addition rather than multiplication:

```{r}
#| echo: true
log(.25) + log(.25) + log(.75) + log(.25) + log(.25) + log(.25) + log(.75)  + log(.25)

```

:::

::: fragment

And we can always exponentiate to turn a log likelihood back to a likelihood:

```{r}
#| echo: true

exp(-8.89313)

```

:::

## MLE of a proportion

$$
\theta^{\sum{y_i}}(1-\theta)^{n-\sum{y_i}}
$$


::: fragment


Taking the log here turns the multiplication into addition, and the exponentiation into multiplication:

$$
\log L(y|\theta) = (\sum^n_{i=1}y_i) \log(\theta) + (n-\sum^n_{i=1}{y_i}) \log(1-\theta)
$$

:::

## MLE of a proportion

So now we have a function we can use to distinguish good guesses at $\theta$ from bad guesses: we just want to find a parameter that maximizes this function:

$$
\log L(y|\theta) = (\sum^n_{i=1}y_i) \log(\theta) + (n-\sum^n_{i=1}{y_i}) \log(1-\theta)
$$


```{r}
#| echo: true
# 100 responses with p = .26
y<-rep(c(0, 1), c(74, 26))
ll_prop<-function(y, theta){
  n<-length(y)
  sumy<-sum(y)
  ll<-sumy * log(theta) + (n-sumy) * log(1-theta)
  return(ll)
}


ll_prop(y, .5)
ll_prop(y, .4)
ll_prop(y, .8)

```


## MLE of a proportion

Again, we could probably just eyeball this, but to find it mathematically we would need to do a bit of calculus:

```{r}
library(patchwork)

# 1. Define the data/parameters
# Let's assume we observed x successes out of n trials
x <- 26
n <- 100

# Create a data frame over the domain of the proportion p (0 to 1)
# Avoiding exactly 0 and 1 to prevent log(0) errors
p_seq <- seq(0.01, 0.99, length.out = 500)

df <- data.frame(
  p = p_seq,
  log_lik = x * log(p_seq) + (n - x) * log(1 - p_seq),
  derivative = (x / p_seq) - ((n - x) / (1 - p_seq))
)

# Maximum Likelihood Estimate (MLE) for reference lines
mle <- x / n

# 2. Create the Log-Likelihood Plot
p1 <- ggplot(df, aes(x = p, y = log_lik)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2c3e50", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mle, linetype = "dashed", color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "Log-Likelihood Function",
  #  subtitle = paste("Maximum at p =", mle),
    x = "Proportion (p)",
    y = "Log-Likelihood l(p)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

# 3. Create the Derivative (Score Function) Plot
p2 <- ggplot(df, aes(x = p, y = derivative)) +
  geom_line(color = "#16a085", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mle, linetype = "dashed", color = "#e74c3c", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "solid", color = "gray60", linewidth = 0.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Derivative of Log-Likelihood",
   # subtitle = "Equals 0 at the MLE",
    x = "Proportion (p)",
    y = "Score U(p)"
  ) +
  # Constrain y-axis slightly so asymptotes near 0 and 1 don't distort the scale

  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

# 4. Display them side by side using patchwork
p1

```


## MLE of a proportion

The maximum is the point where the derivative (slope) of this line with respect to $\theta$ is 0 (and where the second derivative of this line is negative)



```{r}
p1 + p2



```

## MLE of a proportion

The maximum is the point where the derivative (slope) of this line with respect to $\theta$ is 0 (and where the second derivative of this line is negative)

$$
\log L(y|\theta) = (\sum^n_{i=1}y_i) \log(\theta) + (n-\sum^n_{i=1}{y_i}) \log(1-\theta)
$$

## MLE of a proportion

Simplifying the notation a bit...

$$
\begin{align*}
&Y \log(\theta) + (n-Y) \log(1-\theta)\\
\end{align*}
$$

where $Y = \sum^n_{i=1}{y_i}$

::: fragment


Applying the [chain rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain_rule)

$$
Y \frac{1}{\theta} +  (n-Y) \frac{-1}{1-\theta}
$$

:::

::: fragment

And simplifying...

$$
\frac{d}{d\theta} = \frac{Y}{\theta} +  \frac{(n-Y) }{1-\theta}
$$


:::

## MLE of a proportion


Now we can set it to zero and solve algebraically for $\theta$

$$
0 = \frac{Y}{\theta} +  \frac{(n-Y) }{1-\theta}
$$

. . .


$$
\begin{align}
\frac{Y}{\theta} =  \frac{(n-Y) }{1-\theta}  && \text{Adding } \frac{(n-Y) }{1-\theta} \text{ to both sides} \\
Y(1-\theta) =(n-Y)\theta   && \text{cross multiplying by } \theta(1-\theta)\\ 
Y-Y\theta  = n\theta - Y\theta && \text{Expanding}\\
Y = n\theta  && \text{Cancelling } -Y\theta\\ 
\theta = \frac{Y}{n} && \text{Solving for } \theta
\end{align}
$$


## MLE of a proportion

What is the population probability of Bigfoot belief ($\theta$) that is [most likely]{.yellow} to have generated a sample with 26% Bigfoot believers?

. . .

The estimate of $\theta$ that maximizes the likelihood of observing our data is just the sample proportion: .26!

$$
\begin{align*}
\hat{\theta} = \frac{Y}{n}  \\
\end{align*}
$$


## MLE with a model

The answer in this example was kind of obvious to begin with, but Maximum Likelihood Estimation is useful because it gives us a flexible way to judge models when we can't rely on an easy metric like the sum of squared errors.

. . .

For instance, $\theta$ could be a set of coefficient values in a regression instead of a single average:


$$
\begin{align*}
L(y|\theta, X) =  \prod^n_{i=1} p ^{y_i} (1-p)^{1-y_i} \\
p = \frac{1}{1+e^{-(\theta'X)}}
\end{align*}
$$


::: fragment

We've definitely made the problem here more complex, but the goal is the same: we want to find parameters for $\theta$ that maximize the likelihood of our observed data.

:::


## MLE with a model



::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
So, with a simple dataset of 10 observations, we need to come up with two parameter values ($\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$) that maximize the likelihood of the data.

$$
\begin{align*}
L(y|\theta, X) =  \prod^n_{i=1} p ^{y_i} (1-p)^{1-y_i} \\
p = \frac{1}{1+e^{-(\theta'X)}}
\end{align*}
$$

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}


data<-tribble(
  ~"id", ~"x", ~"y", 
    1,   -2.5,  0 ,
    2,   -1.8,  0 ,
    3,   -1.2,  0 ,
    4,   -0.5,  0 ,
    5,   -0.1,  1 ,
    6,    0.4,  0 ,
    7,    0.9,  1 ,
    8,    1.6,  1 ,
    9,    2.2,  1 ,
    10,   3.0,  1 )

knitr::kable(data)


```

:::
:::::


## MLE with a model



::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

- Let's try $\beta_0 = 1$ and $\beta_1 = 2$

- Plugging that in to observation 1 gives us: $p = \frac{1}{1+e^{-(1 + 2\times-2.5)}} = 0.018$

- The likelihood for observation 1 under these values is $L(y_i|\beta, X_i) =  0.018 ^{0} (1-0.018)^{1-0} = 0.982$

- The log likelihood of this observation is $\ln(0.982) = -0.0180$


:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}


data<-tribble(
  ~"id", ~"x", ~"y",
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// 2. Mock dataset of 20 real-world styled binary outcome observations
sampleData = [
  { id: 1,  x: -2.5, y: 0 },
  { id: 2,  x: -1.8, y: 0 },
  { id: 3,  x: -1.2, y: 0 },
  { id: 4,  x: -0.5, y: 0 },
  { id: 5,  x: -0.1, y: 1 }, // Inflection zone mixing begins
  { id: 6,  x:  0.4, y: 0 },
  { id: 7,  x:  0.9, y: 1 },
  { id: 8,  x:  1.6, y: 1 },
  { id: 9,  x:  2.2, y: 1 },
  { id: 10, x:  3.0, y: 1 }
]

// 3. Compute dynamic row valuations and overall Log Likelihood
evaluatedData = sampleData.map(row => {
  const linearPredictor = beta0 + beta1 * row.x;
  const p = 1 / (1 + Math.exp(-linearPredictor));
  
  // Boundary safety clamp for math log stability near 0 or 1
  const pClamped = Math.max(0.00001, Math.min(0.99999, p));
  const Likelihood = row.y === 1 ? pClamped : 1 - pClamped;
  const logLikelihood = row.y === 1 ? Math.log(pClamped) : Math.log(1 - pClamped);

  return {
    "Obs ID": row.id,
    "Predictor (X)": row.x.toFixed(1),
    "Observed Outcome (Y)": row.y,
    "Predicted Prob (P)": p.toFixed(3),
    "Likelihood": Likelihood.toFixed(3),
    "Log Likelihood": logLikelihood.toFixed(3)
  };
})

// 4. Calculate total log likelihood score sum
totalLogLikelihood = evaluatedData.reduce((sum, row) => sum + parseFloat(row["Log Likelihood"]), 0)

// 5. Output the responsive HTML dynamic grid table with summary line
viewof dynamicTable = Inputs.table(evaluatedData, {
  columns: ["Predictor (X)", "Observed Outcome (Y)", "Predicted Prob (P)","Likelihood", "Log Likelihood"],
  header: {
    "Obs ID": "ID",
    "Predictor (X)": "X",
    "Observed Outcome (Y)": "Y",
    "Predicted Prob (P)": "Predicted P(Y=1)",
    "Likelihood" : "Likelihood",
    "Log Likelihood": "LogLik"
  },
//  layout: "fixed",
  required: false,                                 // Stripped out row selection checkboxes
  width: "90%",
  height: "50%",
  select: false

})
```

```{ojs}
// 3. Keep sliders clean and independent for perfect manual dragging
viewof beta0 = Inputs.range([-5, 5], {value: 1.5, step: 0.01, label: html`<b>Intercept (β₀)</b>`})
viewof beta1 = Inputs.range([0.1, 5], {value: 0.5, step: 0.01, label: html`<b>Slope (β₁)</b>`})

// 4. Fixed Click Handler: Mutates element node values directly and fires native change inputs
solveButton = {
  const btn = html`<button style="font-size: 0.6rem; padding: 2px 6px; font-weight: bold; background: #2c7bb6; color: white; border: none; border-radius: 3px; cursor: pointer;">Solve MLE</button>`;
  btn.onclick = () => {
    // Look up the underlying html element instances directly
    const input0 = viewof beta0.querySelector("input[type=range]");
    const input1 = viewof beta1.querySelector("input[type=range]");
    
    if (input0 && input1) {
      // Reassign values directly
      viewof beta0.value = -0.4255;
      viewof beta1.value = 2.4870;
      
      // Dispatch standard DOM events to tell OJS that slider inputs shifted
      viewof beta0.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true}));
      viewof beta1.dispatchEvent(new Event("input", {bubbles: true}));
    }
  };
  return btn;
}
```

## MLE with a model

So how do we find the right parameters here without guesswork?

$$
\begin{align*}
L(y|\theta, X) =  \prod^n_{i=1} p ^{y_i} (1-p)^{1-y_i} \\
p = \frac{1}{1+e^{-(\theta'X)}}
\end{align*}
$$

::: fragment
Just like the previous case, we would find the (partial) derivative of the log likelihood function with respect to each parameter, set to zero, and solve:

$$
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\beta_1} = \sum{^n_{i=1}}\left( y_i-\frac{1}{1+e^{-(\beta_0 +\beta_1X_i)}} \right) X
$$

:::



## MLE with a model


::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
However, unlike the previous case, **we can't find solve this algebraically**, so the parameters here are approximated using a numeric algorithm (R's GLM function uses [iteratively reweighted least squares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iteratively_reweighted_least_squares))
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: fragment

![](../images/irwls_slow_fixed.gif)

:::
:::
:::::


## Back where we started




```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
lm(repvote_numeric ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE,data= chep_subset)

```


::: fragment

The formula syntax remains the same, but the use the `glm` function and we specify a logit link with `family=binomial(link='logit')`

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

glm(repvote_numeric ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE,data= chep_subset, 
    family=binomial(link='logit'))



```
:::


::: fragment
Or the probit link with  `family=binomial(link='probit')`

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true


glm(repvote_numeric ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE,data= chep_subset, 
    family=binomial(link='probit'))
```

:::


## Back where we started: logit model


::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Unlike a linear model, GLM coefficients typically lack a straightforward interpretation.

- In the case of the logit model, each coefficient represents the effect of a one unit increase in that variable on the logged odds ratio: $\log \left( \frac{p}{1-p}\right)$

- On this scale, positive values correspond to an increasing probability, and negative values mean decreasing probability, but there's less that can be said beyond this.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {style="font-size: 85%;"}

```{r}
#| echo: false


m1<-lm(repvote_numeric ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE,data= chep_subset)
m2<-glm(repvote_numeric ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE,data= chep_subset, 
    family=binomial(link='logit'))
m3<-glm(repvote_numeric ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE,data= chep_subset, 
    family=binomial(link='probit'))


mlist<-list("logit" = m2, "probit" = m3)
mod<-modelsummary(list("Logit" = m2), 
             
             coef_rename = TRUE,
             fmt = 3,  
             statistic = "conf.int",  
             gof_map = c("nobs"), # showing only selected fit stats
             output = 'gt'
)
```


```{r}

gtsave(mod, '../images/votelogit.png')

knitr::include_graphics("../images/votelogit.png")


```


:::

:::
:::::



## Back where we started: logit model


::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Exponentiating the coefficient values will turn $\log \left( \frac{p}{1-p}\right)$ into $\frac{p}{1-p})$

- On this scale, each coefficient corresponds to *multiplying* the odds of y=1. So a one unit increase in the Financial Hardship index means cutting the odds of voting for the Republican candidate in the House by .9. (a $(0.933-1) \times 100 = -6.7\%$ decrease in the odds)

- This is still not an especially intuitive interpretation.

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {style="font-size: 85%;"}

```{r}
#| echo: false


m1<-lm(repvote_numeric ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE,data= chep_subset)
m2<-glm(repvote_numeric ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE,data= chep_subset, 
    family=binomial(link='logit'))
m3<-glm(repvote_numeric ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE,data= chep_subset, 
    family=binomial(link='probit'))


mlist<-list("logit" = m2, "probit" = m3)
mod<-modelsummary(list("Logit (exponentiated)" = m2), 
             exponentiate = TRUE,
             coef_rename = TRUE,
             fmt = 3,  
             statistic = "conf.int",  
             gof_map = c("nobs"), # showing only selected fit stats
             output = 'gt'
)
```


```{r}

gtsave(mod, '../images/votelogit_exp.png')

knitr::include_graphics("../images/votelogit_exp.png")


```


:::

:::
:::::



## Logit probabilities

- We can also transform logit regression values back into predicted probabilities.

- To do this, we would first get a linear prediction for a particular scenario and then transform it back into a probability using the logistic function: $\frac{1}{1+e^{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2...)}}$

## Logit probabilities

For instance: what is the probability of a Republican House vote for someone with 3 financial hardships who voted for Trump in 2024? 

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

Start by getting the linear prediction:

:::

:::: {.r-stack}

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="2" .fade-in-then-out}


$$
\begin{aligned}
\eta &= -3.25\ - \\
&\quad 0.07(\operatorname{HARDSHIP\_INDEX})\ + \\
&\quad 5.42(\operatorname{VOTE24\_CHOICE}_{\operatorname{(2)\ Donald\ Trump}})\ + \\
&\quad 2.53(\operatorname{VOTE24\_CHOICE}_{\operatorname{(3)\ Someone\ else}})\ + \\
&\quad 2.86(\operatorname{VOTE24\_CHOICE}_{\operatorname{(4)\ Did\ not\ vote}})
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="3"}


$$
\begin{aligned}
\eta &= -3.25\ - \\
&\quad 0.07(3)\ + \\
&\quad 5.42(1)\ + \\
&\quad 2.53(0)\ + \\
&\quad 2.86(0) \\
= 1.96
\end{aligned}
$$

:::


::::

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}



::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="4"}

Then transform it using the logistic function:

:::


::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="5"}



$$
\frac{1}{e^{-(1.96)}} = 0.88
$$



:::

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="6"}

The model predicts an 88% chance of voting Republican.

:::



:::
:::::


## Logit probabilities

Notice here that the effects of HARDSHIP_INDEX, on the probability scale, are not constant. They get slightly stronger as we move toward P=.5


::: {style="font-size: 70%;"}


```{r}

df<-data.frame(VOTE24_CHOICE = "(2) Donald Trump", 
               HARDSHIP_INDEX = 0:13)

df$pred<-predict(m2, newdata=df, type='response')
df|>
  rename(Prediction = pred)|>
  mutate(Prediction = round(Prediction, digits=3))|>
  mutate(`Change from previous` = Prediction - lag(Prediction))|>
  knitr::kable(align='c')
  

```

:::


## Back where we started: logit model

Ideally, we would like to be able to interpret the effects in terms of probabilities, but the effect of each variable on the probability scale is not linear. In the next class, we'll talk about some ways to handle this, as well as how to assess models and use other types of GLMs.

```{r}
library(ggeffects)
preds<-predict_response(m2, terms=c('HARDSHIP_INDEX', 'VOTE24_CHOICE'))
preds|>
 # filter(group == "(2) Donald Trump")|>
  plot() +
  labs(y="% chance of voting Republican in 2026",
       title ='',
       x = "Financial Hardship Index"
       )+
  facet_wrap(~group, scales='free') +
  scale_color_manual(values=c("blue","#DC143C", "purple", "grey")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("blue","#DC143C", "purple", "grey")) +
  heiss_theme+
      theme(legend.position = "none") 






```




## R-code


If you're interested in playing around with NORC's Civic Health Poll, you can access the whole file using the code below:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
library(tidyverse)
library(haven)
fname<-here::here("Data", "chep.zip")
if(!file.exists(fname)){
  download.file('https://civichealth.norc.org/downloads/civichealth_datafile.zip',
                mode='wb',
                dest=fname
  )
}

chep<-read_dta(unz(fname, filename='civichealth_datafile.dta' ))

# Converting stata formatted variables to factors
chep_fac<-chep|>
  as_factor()

# https://civichealth.norc.org/index.html for more info on the data

```


## R-code

Running the logistic regression on example data:

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
library(tidyverse)
# pre-filtered and formatted subset of the data
chep_subset<-readRDS(here::here("Data", "chep_subset.rds"))

model<-glm(
  REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE ,
  family = binomial(link='logit'),
  data = chep_subset)
summary(model)
# getting predictions on the response scale for different values of the predictors:

# 1. create a data frame with combinations of the predictors:
df<-expand.grid(VOTE24_CHOICE = c("(1) Kamala Harris","(2) Donald Trump",
                                  "(3) Someone else", "(4) Did not vote"
                                  ), 
               HARDSHIP_INDEX = 0:13)

#2. use predict on the model object with the newdata and type='response' options:
df$prediction<-predict(model, 
        newdata= df,
        type='response'
        )

ggplot(df, aes(x=HARDSHIP_INDEX, y=prediction,
               color =VOTE24_CHOICE 
               )) + geom_line() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  labs(y='Probability of voting for Republican',
       x = "Number of financial hardships",
       subtitle = "Number of financial hardships in the last year",
       caption = "Source: NORC Civic Health & Elections Project 2026",
       color = '2024 Presidential Vote'
       ) +
    scale_color_manual(values=c("blue","#DC143C", "purple", "grey"))

  


```
